title: StateBits: A Recall Benchmark for Quantized Recurrent States in Linear-Attention and Hybrid Language Models
affiliations: School of Electrical Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence, POSTECH, Pohang, Republic of Korea
abstract: Linear-attention, state-space and hybrid language models keep a fixed-size recurrent state that is rewritten at every decoding step, and serving systems increasingly store it in eight bits or fewer. Existing evaluations of state quantization measure perplexity or short-context accuracy. We introduce StateBits, a benchmark that measures how quantized recurrent states affect long-context recall. StateBits covers fourteen released models with diagonal and delta-rule recurrences, from 1.3B to 48B parameters, contexts from 4K to 128K tokens, seven storage formats, and a fidelity metric, answer-token agreement with the same model using an FP32 state, that is defined even where the model's own recall is poor. Three findings stand out. First, recall breaks before perplexity: with per-row INT8 states, 9 of 14 models keep PG-19 perplexity within 0.01 nats of FP32 at 8K tokens, but only 3 keep recall agreement above 0.98. Second, at equal width, stochastic rounding and BF16 dominate round-to-nearest integers and FP8 at long context. Third, the bits needed for faithful recall grow linearly in the logarithm of the context length, with a pooled precision doubling cost (PDC) of 0.87 bits per state entry per doubling (95% CI 0.85-0.89) that is nearly the same for diagonal and delta-rule models. The benchmark, prompts and per-model results are publicly released.

blocks.text: Hybrid language models that replace most attention layers with linear attention or state-space layers are now deployed at scale [⟦kimi⟧, ⟦qwen35⟧, ⟦nemoh⟧, ⟦nemo3⟧]. Their recurrent layers keep a state of fixed size, but that state is read and written at every decoding step and has to be kept for every request and every cached prefix [⟦marconi⟧, ⟦dasc⟧]. Quantizing it is the obvious way to cut both memory traffic and footprint, and several recent works do so for selective SSMs [⟦quamba2⟧, ⟦qmamba⟧] and for delta-rule models [⟦damp⟧, ⟦kozyrev⟧].

A recurrent state is an unusual quantization target. Every write starts from the previously quantized state, so rounding errors are fed back and can persist for as long as the channel that holds them retains information [⟦damp⟧, ⟦veldhuis⟧]. The damage therefore depends on how long the model runs on a quantized state, and an evaluation at a few thousand tokens can miss it. It also depends on what is measured. Most evaluations use perplexity or short-answer accuracy [⟦quamba2⟧, ⟦qmamba⟧, ⟦veldhuis⟧], which are dominated by local predictions. Long-context use, in contrast, is often limited by recall: the ability to retrieve a specific item written into the state many thousands of tokens earlier [⟦zoology⟧, ⟦arora⟧, ⟦jelassi⟧].

We introduce StateBits, a benchmark for the effect of state quantization on long-context recall. StateBits evaluates fourteen released models spanning pure SSMs, gated linear attention, delta-rule models and hybrids, at contexts from 4K to 128K tokens and in seven storage formats. Its central metric is answer-token agreement: the fraction of answer tokens on which the model with a quantized state makes the same greedy prediction as the same model with an FP32 state. Agreement isolates the effect of the storage format from the model's own recall ability, so it remains informative for small models whose FP32 recall at 128K tokens is weak.

Our contributions are: (1) the benchmark, a reference harness, and results for 14 models × 6 lengths × 7 formats (Section 3); (2) evidence that recall degrades at widths where perplexity is still essentially unchanged (Section 4.1); (3) a comparison of formats and rounding rules at long context (Section 4.2); (4) an analysis of delta-rule erasure (Section 4.3); and (5) a fit of the bits needed for faithful recall as a function of context length across all fourteen models, which yields a single per-doubling cost that holds across recurrence types (Section 4.4).

Recurrent and hybrid models. Linear attention [⟦katha⟧] and its gated variants [⟦gla⟧] summarize the past in a matrix-valued state; Mamba and Mamba-2 [⟦mamba⟧, ⟦mamba2⟧] do so with selective state-space updates, and delta-rule models add an erasure along the current key [⟦deltanet⟧, ⟦gdn⟧, ⟦gdn2⟧, ⟦rwkv7⟧]. Hybrids interleave such layers with attention [⟦zamba2⟧, ⟦falconh1⟧, ⟦nemoh⟧, ⟦nemonano2⟧, ⟦kimi⟧, ⟦qwen35⟧]. Recent analyses examine how these models store and retrieve facts in the state [⟦afendulev⟧, ⟦koren⟧, ⟦boesch⟧, ⟦cheng⟧], how long-term recall separates from short-range stability [⟦cao⟧], and how state anomalies arise at extreme lengths [⟦sane⟧]. Several studies question whether recurrent layers deliver long-context recall at all compared with simple alternatives [⟦jolicoeur⟧, ⟦fountzoulas⟧]. Uncertainty-aware updates have also been proposed for the write itself [⟦kdn⟧].

State and cache quantization. Quamba2 and Q-Mamba quantize the cached state of selective SSMs to eight bits [⟦quamba2⟧, ⟦qmamba⟧]. DAMP protects slowly decaying channels of GDN and KDA states with higher precision and stores the rest in INT8 [⟦damp⟧], and dasc drops short-horizon units from prefix checkpoints [⟦dasc⟧]. Nemotron 3 stores Mamba states in FP16 with stochastic rounding [⟦nemo3⟧], and four-bit weights and activations have been applied to the recurrent half of hybrid models [⟦kozyrev⟧]. For attention, KV-cache quantization [⟦kivi⟧, ⟦kvquant⟧, ⟦turboquant⟧] faces a related but easier problem, because cache entries are written once. Prefix caching for hybrids [⟦marconi⟧, ⟦tailreplay⟧] stores states as well, usually in full precision. On the context-length dependence, Veldhuis et al. [⟦veldhuis⟧] showed that the width needed to keep perplexity within a fixed tolerance of an FP32 state grows with the logarithm of the context, which they call the bit-growth law; we return to it in Section 4.4. Why post-training quantization works at all for large models is itself an open question [⟦chenptq⟧].

Long-context recall benchmarks. Needle-in-a-haystack tests and their extensions such as RULER [⟦ruler⟧] and BABILong [⟦babilong⟧] measure whether a model retrieves information at a given depth. Synthetic associative recall tasks [⟦zoology⟧] probe the same ability in a controlled setting. StateBits reuses these task families but changes the target of measurement from the model to the storage format.

StateBits contains fourteen released checkpoints (Table 1). Eight have diagonal or scalar decay and no erasure: Mamba-2 1.3B and 2.7B [⟦mamba2⟧], Falcon-Mamba-7B [⟦falconmamba⟧], GLA-1.3B [⟦gla⟧], and the hybrids Zamba2-2.7B [⟦zamba2⟧], Nemotron-H-8B [⟦nemoh⟧], Falcon-H1-1.5B [⟦falconh1⟧] and Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 [⟦nemonano2⟧]. Six use a delta-rule update: DeltaNet-1.3B [⟦deltanet⟧], Gated DeltaNet-1.3B [⟦gdn⟧], RWKV-7 1.5B [⟦rwkv7⟧], and the hybrids Qwen3.5-9B [⟦qwen35⟧], Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [⟦qwen36⟧] and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct [⟦kimi⟧]. In hybrids only the recurrent layers are quantized; the attention KV cache stays in BF16. Short convolution states are kept in BF16 for all models.

Each model is evaluated at six context lengths, T ∈ {4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K}, with 200 prompts per length: 100 multi-key needle prompts and 50 passkey prompts generated with the RULER templates [⟦ruler⟧], and 50 synthetic key-value retrieval prompts in which 64 key-value pairs are spread uniformly over the context and four are queried at the end. We also run BABILong qa1-qa3 [⟦babilong⟧] at the same lengths as a natural-text check. Prompts are tokenized with each model's own tokenizer and padded with PG-19 [⟦pg19⟧] filler text to the target length.

For every prompt we first run the model with an FP32 state and record its greedy answer. We then run the model with a quantized state, teacher-forcing the FP32 answer, and count the answer tokens on which the quantized model's argmax agrees with the FP32 model's. Answer-token agreement is the mean of this fraction over prompts. Because the reference is the model itself, agreement is defined and informative even when FP32 recall is low; at 128K tokens the FP32 multi-key accuracy of the 1.3B models is below 20%, but their quantized states can still be more or less faithful to the FP32 computation. A model meets the recall criterion at width b and length T if its agreement is at least 0.98. For comparison we also measure the excess NLL on 32 PG-19 books, using the criterion of Veldhuis et al. [⟦veldhuis⟧]: excess NLL at most 0.01 nats over positions (T/2, T].

We evaluate seven formats: BF16 and FP8 (E4M3, per-row FP32 scale) with round-to-nearest, per-row symmetric INT8 with round-to-nearest (rtn) and with stochastic rounding (sr), MXFP6 and per-row INT6 [⟦mx⟧], and NVFP4 with 16-element blocks [⟦fouroversix⟧]. Integer formats use one FP16 absmax scale per row of the state, where a row is one key channel of one head. For the context-length fits in Section 4.4 we additionally sweep per-row INT-b with rtn from 5 to 14 bits in half-bit steps, mixing row widths for fractional values, which is the format used in [⟦veldhuis⟧].

The state is quantized after every token, both during prefill and during the answer. This is stricter than serving systems that process the prompt in chunks and store the state only at chunk boundaries, and it isolates the per-token decoding regime in which errors accumulate fastest. Section 4.2 reports one chunked variant.

Pure recurrent models run with the recurrent kernels of flash-linear-attention [⟦fla⟧] and the mamba_ssm reference implementation; hybrids run through their released Hugging Face implementations [⟦hf⟧] with the recurrent step replaced by our quantizing step kernel. We verified for every model that the step kernel with an FP32 state reproduces the reference logits to within 10^-4 at every position. Models up to 9B parameters run on single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct run with tensor parallelism over four A100 80GB GPUs. The complete benchmark took about 9,400 GPU-hours.

Table 2 counts, for per-row INT8 states with rtn, how many of the fourteen models meet each criterion at each length. At 4K tokens the two criteria nearly agree. Already at 8K they diverge: 9 models keep perplexity within 0.01 nats, but only 3 (DeltaNet-1.3B, Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and RWKV-7 1.5B) keep agreement at or above 0.98. From 16K tokens on, no model meets the recall criterion with an INT8 state, while four still meet the perplexity criterion.

Criterion | 4K | 8K | 16K | 32K | 64K | 128K
excess NLL ≤ 0.01 nats | 13 | 9 | 4 | 1 | 0 | 0
agreement ≥ 0.98 | 11 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0
Table 2: Number of models (of 14) that meet each criterion with per-row INT8 states (rtn, requantized every token).

The gap has a simple interpretation. Most next-token predictions in book text depend on the last few hundred tokens, which are held in quickly decaying channels whose quantization error saturates. A recall query depends on a few slowly decaying channels that carry the needle across the whole context. Their error keeps growing, and a small perturbation of exactly those channels flips the answer while hardly changing the average NLL. The same mechanism explains why mixed-precision schemes that protect slowly decaying channels work well [⟦damp⟧].

Agreement failures are not uniform across task types. At 16K tokens with INT8 states, the synthetic key-value task fails first (mean agreement 0.88), followed by multi-key needles (0.92), passkeys (0.97) and BABILong (0.95). Passkeys are easier because the answer is a short digit string that the model can copy with high confidence.

Table 3 compares the seven formats at 16K tokens, averaged over the fourteen models. BF16, which keeps an 8-bit significand with a per-element exponent, gives the highest agreement, closely followed by INT8 with stochastic rounding. INT8 with rtn is clearly worse, and FP8 E4M3, with only three mantissa bits, is far worse than INT8 despite its dynamic range. Six-bit formats and NVFP4 are not usable at this length without further measures such as mixed precision or outlier handling.
Table 3: Mean answer-token agreement over the fourteen models for each state format, per-token requantization. Bits per entry include scale overhead.

The gap between rtn and sr widens with context length (0.02 at 16K, 0.12 at 64K), consistent with rtn discarding updates smaller than half a step, so that its error grows like a drift rather than a random walk [⟦croci⟧, ⟦gupta⟧]. Quantizing the state only once every 64 tokens, as in chunked prefill, raises INT8 rtn agreement at 64K from 0.74 to 0.90; per-token requantization during the answer then accounts for most of the remaining loss.

Delta-rule models remove part of the state along the current key before writing [⟦deltanet⟧, ⟦gdn⟧], which also removes the component of accumulated rounding error along that key. One might therefore expect delta-rule states to tolerate lower precision. At short context they do: averaged over models, the width needed for faithful recall at 4K tokens is 7.53 bits for the six delta-rule models and 7.75 bits for the eight diagonal ones, and the three models that meet the recall criterion at 8K with INT8 are all non-hybrid delta-rule models.

The advantage does not grow with context. Error components orthogonal to the keys that are written later are never erased, and in a long context with diverse keys most of the accumulated error lies in such directions. As a result the required width grows at nearly the same rate for both families (Section 4.4): the gap between the family means is 0.2 bits at 4K and 0.4 bits at 128K, far from what the erasure of all accumulated error would give.

sections.title: 4.4 Context-length scaling: the precision doubling cost

blocks.text: For every model and length we find b*_R(T), the smallest per-row INT-b width with rtn at which the model meets the recall criterion, interpolating agreement linearly in b between grid points. Table 4 lists b*_R at 4K and 128K tokens. For every model b*_R grows close to linearly in log2 T, and we summarize this growth by the precision doubling cost (PDC): the number of additional bits per state entry needed to keep recall faithful when the context doubles. The PDC is the slope κ of the bit-growth law of Veldhuis et al. [⟦veldhuis⟧], b*(T) = b_0 + κ log2 T, which they fitted with their perplexity criterion on five checkpoints up to 32K tokens and found κ = 0.62 bits per doubling. We use a separate name because we measure it with a recall criterion and over a longer range, and because the per-doubling reading is the one practitioners need.

Table 4: Required width for faithful recall (agreement ≥ 0.98; per-row INT-b, rtn, per-token requantization) and precision doubling cost (bits per state entry per doubling of context), from a least-squares fit of Eq. (1) to six lengths from 4K to 128K. Pooled values use a common slope with per-model intercepts.

The pooled PDC is 0.87 bits per doubling (95% CI 0.85-0.89, bootstrap over models and prompts). Per-model values range from 0.82 to 0.91, and the families differ by only 0.02 (0.88 for diagonal, 0.86 for delta-rule models), which is within the uncertainty. On the four checkpoints shared with Veldhuis et al. [⟦veldhuis⟧] (Mamba-2 1.3B and 2.7B, Falcon-Mamba-7B and GLA-1.3B) our recall-based PDC is 0.82-0.91, clearly above their perplexity-based pooled value of 0.62. Residuals of the per-model fits are below 0.2 bits everywhere, with no visible curvature up to 128K tokens.

Why is the recall-based slope steeper? In the simple model of Veldhuis et al., an unbiased random walk of rounding errors costs 0.5 bits per doubling and coherent drift costs one bit, and channels whose time constant is shorter than the context saturate and stop contributing. Perplexity averages over all channels and is dominated by the saturated, short-lived ones. Recall depends on the slow channels that carry the needle, which have not saturated at any length we test, and under rtn their error is close to a drift, so the slope moves toward one bit. Consistent with this, the slope with stochastic rounding, measured on six models, is lower (0.71 pooled) but still above the perplexity-based value.

For deployments that depend on long-context retrieval we therefore recommend budgeting state precision with the recall-based PDC of 0.87 rather than with the perplexity-based slope. As a rule of thumb, a format that is faithful at 4K tokens loses that property after about one doubling per 0.87 bits of headroom; a model that needs 7.7 bits at 4K needs about 12 bits at 128K.

Agreement is measured with teacher forcing. To check that it predicts end-task behaviour, we also let six models generate freely on BABILong qa1-qa3 at 32K tokens with INT8 rtn and BF16 states. The drop in task accuracy relative to FP32 correlates with one minus agreement across models and formats (Pearson 0.83). In free-running mode a single disagreeing token can derail the answer, so accuracy losses are on average 1.6 times larger than the disagreement rate.

For four models (Mamba-2 2.7B, GLA-1.3B, Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Qwen3.5-9B) we located the state entries responsible for disagreements by restoring FP32 precision in one group of rows at a time. Groups are formed by sorting rows by their mean retention over the prompt. Restoring the slowest-decaying 10% of rows recovers between 61% and 78% of the lost agreement at 32K tokens, whereas restoring the fastest-decaying 50% recovers less than 10%. In the two hybrids we tested this way, the recurrent layers directly after the first attention layer account for a disproportionate share of failures, in line with analyses that find recurrent layers carrying retrieval keys between attention layers [⟦afendulev⟧, ⟦cheng⟧].

This pattern supports precision allocation by decay, as in DAMP [⟦damp⟧]. It also suggests why a fixed allocation calibrated at short context can fail later: the set of rows that matter for recall is small, and their precision requirement grows with length while the rest of the state saturates.

Serving systems choose one state format for all requests. Our results suggest three practical rules. First, validate state formats with a recall-sensitive metric at the longest context the deployment supports; perplexity at a few thousand tokens is not a sufficient test. Second, prefer stochastic rounding or chunked write-back when an integer format is used for decoding, since round-to-nearest loses most at long context. Third, when memory must be saved, spend the bits on slowly decaying rows rather than lowering precision uniformly. StateBits makes each of these checks cheap to run: a full evaluation of one model and one format takes between 4 and 60 GPU-hours depending on model size.

StateBits measures fidelity to the FP32-state model, not task accuracy, and most numbers are teacher-forced. The fits in Section 4.4 use one format family (per-row integers) and per-token requantization; chunked write-back and mixed-precision allocation shift the intercepts substantially and may change the slopes. We did not evaluate models above 48B parameters or contexts beyond 128K tokens. Two further hybrids we tried could not be verified against their reference logits with our step kernel and are not included. Finally, our prompts are synthetic retrieval tasks plus BABILong; recall in agentic or multi-document settings may stress the state differently.

StateBits shows that recurrent-state quantization should be judged by recall at the deployment length. Recall fails before perplexity, round-to-nearest formats degrade fastest, delta-rule erasure helps only at short context, and the width needed for faithful recall grows by a nearly universal 0.87 bits per doubling of context across fourteen models. We hope the benchmark makes it easy to place new state formats and allocation schemes on the same axes.

Multi-key needles follow the RULER niah_multikey_2 template: the haystack consists of distractor key-value sentences, one of which holds the queried key, and the answer is a seven-digit number. Passkeys follow the niah_single_1 template with a five-digit passkey. The synthetic key-value task places 64 pairs of random two-token keys and four-digit values at uniformly random depths, separated by PG-19 filler, and asks for four of them in sequence. All needles are placed at depths drawn uniformly from 10% to 90% of the context. Prompts are generated once per tokenizer family and shared by all models with that tokenizer.

For BABILong we use the released qa1-qa3 splits at 4K-128K and score agreement on the single-word answer. Because BABILong answers are short and drawn from a small vocabulary, its agreement saturates faster than for the numeric needles.

Agreement is evaluated on a half-bit grid of widths. We locate the crossing of 0.98 by linear interpolation between the bracketing widths; interpolating in logit(agreement) instead changes b*_R by at most 0.05 bits. Eq. (1) is fitted by least squares to the six lengths of each model. The pooled fit uses a common slope and one intercept per model. Confidence intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap replicates that resample prompts within each model and length, and resample models for the pooled values. Dropping the 128K point changes the pooled PDC by less than 0.02 bits per doubling, and dropping the 4K point by less than 0.03.

At 128K tokens, three models (Falcon-Mamba-7B, Nemotron-H-8B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) reach the agreement criterion only at 12.5 bits or more, where the FP16 per-row scale starts to limit precision for rows with a large dynamic range. Rerunning those cells with FP32 scales changed b*_R by less than 0.1 bits, so we keep FP16 scales throughout.
